chunks: Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Imran al-Daqqaq (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Muhammad ibn Abi 'Abd Allah narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from some of his companions, from al-Bakr ibn Salih, from Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Muhammad, from Khalid ibn Yazid, from al-'Ala', from Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him) who said:

The Name of Allah is other than Allah Himself. Everything upon which a name falls is created, except for Allah. As for what is expressed by tongues or written by hands, it is created. Allah is the ultimate goal of all His goals. The 'aimed-at' is other than the 'goal'. The goal is described, and everything described is created. The Maker of things is not described with a named limit. He was not formed so that His essence could be known by the making of others, nor did He reach a limit that would be other than Him. He is never humiliated who understands this ruling forever, and it is pure Tawhid (Divine Unity). So observe it, believe it, and understand it with Allah's permission. Whoever claims that he knows Allah through a veil or an image or a likeness, he is a polytheist, because the veil, the likeness, and the image are other than Him. And He is the One, the Unified. So how can one affirm Unity who claims to have known Him through something other than Him? And only he who knows Allah by Allah has known Him. And whoever does not know Him by Him does not know Him; he only knows something other than Him. There is nothing between the Creator and the created. Therefore, Allah is the Creator of things, not from a thing that was. And Allah is named by His Names, and He is other than His Names, and the Names are other than Him.
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between Allah's Name and Allah Himself in Shia theology?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) articulates the doctrine of *Tanzih* (divine transcendence) by distinguishing between the uncreated Essence of Allah and His created names/attributes, noting that any description expressed by tongues or hands is a created entity. This hadith serves as a cornerstone for Shia theological debates against anthropomorphism (*Tashbih*), asserting that true monotheism requires recognizing that the Creator is entirely distinct from creation. Consequently, attributing a form, limit, or example to God constitutes polytheism, as these are 'other' than His pure Unity.
